item.title: Giuliani blasts Mamdani’s 9/11 toxic air blame as buried city records come to light
item.description: Rudy Giuliani's spokesperson accuses Mayor Zohran Mamdani of scoring political points after 170,000 pages of 9/11 toxic air records were released.
item.content:encoded:
Former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani's team is firing back at Mayor Zohran Mamdani after Mamdani accused past city officials of misleading New Yorkers about toxic air following the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks.

Giuliani spokesperson Ted Goodman accused Mamdani of seeking to "score cheap partisan political points" by directing blame toward local officials who rushed to the scene of the attacks while overlooking the radical Islamic terrorists responsible for killing nearly 3,000 people.

"Now would be a good time to remind Mayor Mamdani that cowardly terrorists acting in the name of Islam are 100 percent responsible for all of the death and destruction on September 11, 2001, and for all of the suffering and illness that have continued since that day," Goodman said in a statement to Fox News Digital.

MAMDANI FACES GROWING 9/11 BACKLASH AS OLD POST RESURFACES AHEAD OF GROUND ZERO CEREMONY: 'IS THIS REAL?'

The records released by Mamdani’s administration include more than 170,000 pages documenting the city’s response to the Sept. 11 attacks and their aftermath. The initial release includes 68 boxes of records from the Department of Environmental Protection that were not located until 2025, and records related to 7 World Trade Center.

The records include documents from Giuliani’s administration, including a memo sent to Deputy Mayor Robert Harding that warned the city faced potentially multimillion-dollar lawsuits from New Yorkers who claimed health advisories failed to protect them from toxic exposure and that the sites were inadequately cleaned up.

MAMDANI UNDER FIRE AFTER SYMBOLIC 9/11 PEN GOES TO FORMER AL QAEDA DEFENSE LAWYER

At a news conference announcing the release, Mamdani said the documents showed that officials across multiple administrations had information about hazardous conditions but failed to adequately inform the public.

"I wish there was a limited number of people who misled the public that I could describe them in just a few names," Mamdani said during a Tuesday news conference. "But the truth is that, as we have heard, this goes across a multitude of those that New Yorkers have trusted, and we are here to release these documents today because, for a long time, New Yorkers have known the truth, and yet they have been unable to see the truth in any document that's been presented to them."

Mamdani said the release was intended to give New Yorkers access to records that had been difficult to obtain for years. His administration said the city had settled two lawsuits brought by 9/11 Health Watch as part of the release and created a public portal containing the documents.

"People got sick because the leaders they trusted lied and told them they were safe to breathe in toxic air. And then, when they began to contend with the symptoms of the illnesses that followed, the government that had not hesitated to send them into harm's way was nowhere to be found," Mamdani said.

NYPD CHIEF: 9/11 HEROES’ LEGACY LIVES ON IN EVERY GENERATION OF OFFICERS

Thousands of first responders, residents, workers and others exposed to the World Trade Center site have since developed illnesses recognized by the World Trade Center Health Program as related to 9/11 exposure. The program continues to provide treatment and monitoring for people suffering from certified 9/11-related conditions.

Former Republican New York Gov. George Pataki, who was governor at the time of the attacks, said in an interview with the New York Post this week that he had been diagnosed with restrictive airway disease, which he attributed to his exposure to toxins at Ground Zero.

The newly released records provide additional detail about environmental hazards found in the years after the attacks, including asbestos detected at 15 John Street in Lower Manhattan. The records document asbestos findings at multiple locations and provide additional detail about the city’s environmental response.

The records show that asbestos was detected at some locations at levels below applicable cleanup or exposure benchmarks and at others at levels that appeared to exceed them. Health authorities have said there is no known safe level of asbestos exposure.

Then-EPA Administrator Christie Todd Whitman said in a Sept. 18, 2001, press release that air monitoring results indicated the air near the World Trade Center was safe to breathe, days after the EPA first issued assurances about environmental hazards on Sept. 13.

MAMDANI, NYPD GIVE SECURITY UPDATE AHEAD OF JEWISH HIGH HOLY DAYS, 9/11 25TH ANNIVERSARY

Goodman pointed to the federal government’s role in communicating about air quality after the attacks, noting that the EPA issued public assurances about conditions near Ground Zero. An EPA Inspector General review later concluded that the data available at the time did not fully support the agency’s broad assurances about air safety.

"The EPA, a federal agency, issued press releases and public statements declaring that air samples showed the air quality near Ground Zero was safe," Goodman said, referring to Giuliani's response. "The agency later apologized for those statements, saying it did the best it could with the knowledge available at the time."

Whitman later apologized for the assurances in a 2016 interview, saying she was sorry for people who became sick or died and that she and the EPA had done the best they could with the information available at the time.

The release of the documents follows a petition with more than 100,000 signatures from 9/11 victims' family members requesting that Mamdani not attend the memorial ceremony at Ground Zero Friday.

"This mayor is not serving us," Charles Wolf, who lost his wife on 9/11, said at a noon news conference. "He's serving himself. We are asking respectfully that he not show up."

"Even though there is going to be other politicians there, these are the politicians that helped us push beneficial laws through and literally held our hand during that time," Wolf continued. "Mayor Mamdani has not shown any of that, none of it. He just wants to be there because he wants to be there."

SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

The mayor’s office said the initial release represents only the beginning of the city’s effort to make its 9/11 records publicly accessible, with additional documents expected to be added to the portal.

Eric Mack contributed to this report.

item.title: WWE’s Corey Graves points to these AAA stars who may impress fans at Triplemania 34

AAA and WWE broadcaster Corey Graves spoke to OutKick Dropkick ahead of the event and pointed to a number of Luchadores and wrestlers pro wrestling fans may be impressed by when the dust settles. He first pointed to Mr. Iguana, whose popularity increased when he was showcased during the first WWE-AAA promoted event, Worlds Collide, last year.

"It's interesting to me because I look at it a little differently because I look at it from within the wrestling bubble and it's often that I'm pleasantly surprised by what captures people's imaginations that aren't hardcore wrestling people," Graves said.

"Mr. Iguana, if you're not familiar, he is not a physically large competitor. He's an incredible athlete. He's a really dangerous jiu-jitsu master, but the guy paints himself green. He has a stuffed iguana that competes in the ring with him. It's somewhere in the in the world of the circus meets sports entertainment. La Parka will defend the AAA Latin American Championship against Laredo Kid and Mr. Iguana. WWE fans got a taste of what La Parka can bring to the ring when he was featured in the tournament to determine Roman Reigns’ challenger for his World Heavyweight Championship.

"La Parka is another one. El Hijo del Dr. Wagner Jr. I think is going to be a major player in years to come. He's still young, still kind of figuring things out, getting experience under his belt," Graves said. "There are so many."

Graves said he was really interested in the AAA Cruiserweight Championship match that will feature either Rey Fenix or Ricky Saints as the champion going up against Mini Vikingo, Jack Cartwheel and Nathan Frazer in a fatal four-way match.

In particular, it's going to take place on Sunday, the Cruiserweight Championship match. You've got Rey Fenix, Mini Vikingo, Jack Cartwheel, and (Nathan Frazer)," he told OutKick Dropkick.

item.title: Oakland schools in hotseat over 'students of color' program while taking millions in federal funding
item.description: Parents Defending Education filed a Title VI complaint alleging Oakland Unified School District's Latinx mentoring program excludes White students.
item.content:encoded:
FIRST ON FOX — The Oakland Unified School District (OUSD) is in the hot seat over a federally funded "Latinx Mentoring and Achievement Program" that allegedly excludes White students from receiving academic support, mentorship, and cash incentives.

Parents Defending Education (PDE), a national educational rights group, filed a federal civil rights complaint against the district alleging that its Latino Men & Boys (LMB) and Latina Mentoring & Achievement (LMA) programs violate Title VI and Title IX of the Civil Rights Act.

"The Supreme Court has recognized only two compelling interests that permit resort to race-based government action: first, 'remediating specific identified instances of past discrimination that violated the Constitution or a statute,' and second, 'avoiding imminent and serious risks to human safety in prisons, such as a race riot,'" the complaint, sent exclusively to Fox News Digital, states.

CALIFORNIA COUNTY APPROVES REPARATIONS PLAN AS NEIGHBORING SCHOOL DISTRICT 'BLACK THRIVING' EFFORT STALLS

The initiative, nationally recognized by The Obama Foundation, is listed under OUSD’s "Community Partners" webpage and operates in conjunction with The Unity Council — an Oakland-based organization that claims to promote "social equity and enhancing quality of life by creating vibrant communities where everyone can work, learn, and thrive."

According to The Unity Council’s website, the initiatives "are school-based, culturally rooted programs located in selected schools in the Oakland Unified School District." The original LMB program was later expanded to create the LMA program following initial outreach.

"The programs work with Latinx youth ages 12–18 and their families and schools to improve outcomes in mental and physical health, education, and career planning," The Unity Council's site states. "The program significantly increases graduation rates for Latinx youth in Oakland schools and promotes healthy lifestyles, academic focus and leadership development. The program is available for male-identified, female-identified, and non-binary youth."

ERIKA KIRK URGES CONSERVATIVE STUDENTS NOT TO BACK DOWN IN FIRST SCHOOL YEAR SINCE CHARLIE'S ASSASSINATION

However, PDE’s civil rights complaint alleges that because OUSD receives millions in federal financial assistance, offering racially exclusive perks through third-party partners breaches federal nondiscrimination laws.

The complaint further details that the LMB initiative grants direct financial payouts to participating students.

"During the 2024-2025 school year, the Unity Council distributed roughly $3,000 in ‘milestones and stipends’ to minority students through the LMB program," the complaint states. "This is important because the LMB program discriminates against students based on race. For example, OUSD’s 2022-2023 service agreement with the Unity Council says that the LMB program is offered to ‘Latino males and other students of color’ and their families. OUSD’s 2024-2025 service agreement likewise states that the LMB program is meant for ‘approximately two hundred Latino young men and their families.’"

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

"In other words, OUSD pays the Unity Council to run a program that gives tutoring, mentoring, health and wellness programs, and even cash to male minority students — specifically male Latino students," PDE argues in its filing. "But the LMB program does not include White students. Nor does OUSD offer any other similar support program for White OUSD students. Because the program denies these benefits to White students, it discriminates against these students on the basis of race."

Neither OUSD nor The Unity Council immediately responded to Fox News Digital's requests for comment regarding the federal complaint.

"Oakland Unified School District has forgotten that ours is a colorblind Constitution. In a ham-fisted attempt to guarantee student ‘equity’ outcomes, Oakland USD has sponsored a multitude of programs geared toward only one race or sex in violation of federal law," said Sarah Parshall Perry, Vice President and Legal Fellow at Defending Education.

Perry went on to say, "Cash stipends, tutoring assistance, wellness programs, and food and housing benefits for only one group of students, to the exclusion of others, are just the tip of the iceberg in one of California's largest school districts. Discriminating on the basis of race or sex--even when classified as a benign ‘diversity’ effort--is illegal. This Administration has made that abundantly clear, but it seems Oakland is due for a refresher."

item.title: SEAL who killed bin Laden recalls 9/11 moment that changed his life: ‘Welcome to my world’
item.description: Rob O'Neill recalls watching the World Trade Center attacks from a German operations center, where Osama bin Laden and al-Qaida were first named.
item.content:encoded:
Rob O’Neill, the Navy SEAL credited with killing Usama bin Laden, had just returned from a 40-day deployment to Kosovo when the world changed forever.

The former Navy SEAL told Fox News Digital in an interview ahead of the 25th anniversary of 9/11 that he was stationed in Stuttgart, Germany, on Sept. 11, 2001, preparing equipment and catching up on emails when every television channel switched to breaking news.

"At first, there was a hole in the North Tower," O’Neill recalled. "No one even knew what the North Tower of the World Trade Center was that day."

O’Neill and his fellow service members initially wondered whether a small plane had accidentally crashed into the building. But after the second plane struck the South Tower shortly after 9 a.m. Eastern time, they immediately understood the significance of what they were watching.

AMERICA’S HEARTLAND COMES FACE-TO-FACE WITH 9/11 HISTORY AS 25TH ANNIVERSARY NEARS

"I’m in an operations center with intel analysts and Navy SEALs, and we all collectively knew that our lives just changed," O’Neill said.

The names of Usama bin Laden and al-Qaeda were soon mentioned in the room.

"We’re on a deployment to Germany, we’re probably going to Sudan. We don’t know where," he said. "The name Usama bin Laden was said in that room, al-Qaeda. And we just knew our lives were going to change."

O’Neill eventually re-enlisted in the Navy in the aftermath of the attacks and went on to serve with SEAL Team Six, the elite special operations unit that ultimately carried out the raid that killed bin Laden in Pakistan in 2011.

But in the immediate aftermath of 9/11, he did not know he would play a role in hunting down the mastermind of the attacks.

"I knew, for me, the Navy was never going to be a career," O’Neill said. "I joined because I thought it was cool, re-enlisted because of the guys, re-enlisted because of 9/11, go to SEAL Team Six."

As the reality of the attacks set in, O’Neill briefly left the secure operations area and called his brother in Montana, who worked in morning radio.

AS AMERICAN PRIDE HITS A 25-YEAR LOW, A NEW 9/11 EDUCATION PLATFORM URGES THE NATION TO NEVER FORGET

"I said, ‘Hey man, I don’t know if you’re up. Turn the TV on,’" O’Neill recalled. "He said, ‘Which channel?’ I said, ‘Doesn’t matter.’ And then he turned it on and all I said to him was, ‘Welcome to my world.’"

Looking back on the 25 years that have passed since the tragedy that took the lives of 2,977 people, O’Neill says he was moved by the way the country came together after the terrorist attacks and while he hopes there is never another 9/11, he does wish Americans could recapture the spirit of unity that followed. He recalled the image of lawmakers from both parties standing together on the steps of the Capitol and singing "God Bless America."

"It was about America first, not foreign interests," O’Neill said. "It was a time of unity."

Roughly a third of the U.S. population was not alive on 9/11 and O’Neill told Fox News Digital what his message for them about the tragedy would be.

"No matter what, at night, don’t go to bed angry with anyone in your family," he said. "Hug everyone that’s there and tell them you love them."

"You remember on Monday, September 10, some people didn’t do that, and they were jumping out of skyscrapers the next day," O’Neill said.

He urged Americans to focus on their families, neighbors, communities and first responders.

"If you can take care of each other and you master those basics, then the world around you is going to be fine," he said. "Sometimes it’s better just to put the phone down and go outside and look at the sun."

O’Neill said that spending time outside can provide perspective in an increasingly chaotic world.

"You’ll know that you’re not random," he said. "You’re here by design. God loves you. He puts you here on purpose."

O’Neill said the legacy of the attacks and his path from Butte, Montana to the elite SEAL Team 6 is a reminder of the opportunities available to Americans, particularly young people.

"If you want to do something, leave the house," O’Neill said. "You can do anything you want."

"Don’t let the negativity get to you," he added. "At any moment you decide, you can do that."

item.title: Pete Davidson says becoming a dad changed how he views father's death on 9/11
item.description: Pete Davidson revealed this 9/11 anniversary is "extra tough" now that he's the same age his firefighter dad was when he died at the World Trade Center.
item.content:encoded:
Pete Davidson is now the same age — 33 — that his firefighter dad was when he died on 9/11.

"I thought, ‘Oh, he was an old guy. He’s 33,’" Davidson told the New York Post in a recent interview. "But now I’m there, and I have a kid, and that would be like my kid not having her dad."

To mark 25 years since the tragedy, Davidson is participating in a comedy benefit at Madison Square Garden with Jon Stewart.

FOX NEWS MEDIA ANNOUNCES EXTENSIVE 9/11 ANNIVERSARY COVERAGE FROM GROUND ZERO, PENTAGON AND SHANKSVILLE

"So, this year is extra tough, but also extra beautiful because I get to spend the day with Scottie," he said of his daughter who was born last December and is named after his late father. "It’ll be very healing and special."

Davidson shares Scottie with ex-girlfriend Elsie Hewitt.

"It was really cool that Elsie also wanted to name her Scottie," he told the Post. "My dad’s name was Scott, but his nickname was Scotty. When she arrived, we both looked at her and were like, ‘She looks like a Scottie.’ It’s nice to keep that name alive."

The "Saturday Night Live" alum is also looking forward to using the comedy benefit as a way of "reclaim[ing]" the day and just having "fun."

PETE DAVIDSON SAYS YOUNG PEOPLE 'DON'T HAVE A SHOT' AT FINDING LOVE

"And not be in the middle of 12 documentaries that are so sad and rehash it," he added.

Davidson explained on Theo Von’s podcast last year that his dad's crew was the first truck over the bridge to the World Trade Center.

FRANK SILLER: 'I LOVE YOU, BROTHER' -- THE 9/11 LOSS THAT INSPIRED A MISSION OF SERVICE

"So they were the first truck over there and pretty much the whole house died, which is sad, but at least he died with his pals."

Davidson called his dad "f---ing hilarious."

"My memories are few and far between because I was 7, but I just remember laughing a lot, him being pretty jacked and smoking a lot of cigarettes, and driving a Subaru Impreza. That’s all I remember."

He said he also remembers his dad always had a big smile on his face, and old friends who tell Davidson stories about him also light up when they talk about him.

9/11 IS BECOMING HISTORY. MY GENERATION MUST MAKE SURE AMERICA NEVER FORGETS

"I was really young, so I didn’t know what the f--- happened, so it hit me later. Like when I was in college, I was like, ‘Oh, I’m pretty angry about this," he revealed.

"It’s actually super f---ed up, but I have his badge, like his chain and they, and that’s how they --- you know, cause everybody was pretty burnt up, so that’s how they knew it was him. And I have it, and I just keep it in a safe because, like with my luck, I’ll lose that s---."

FORMER 'SATURDAY NIGHT LIVE' STAR PETE DAVIDSON CHECKS INTO WELLNESS CENTER FOR MENTAL HEALTH: REPORT

He said he also has his dad’s jacket, which he used to have on display in his home but decided to take down because it could be a depressing reminder all the time.

Davidson’s mom has pictures of his dad everywhere in her home. He said, "But it’s kind of haunting where you’re just like I would like the option, like if I want to go down memory lane I can, but like just like to have your dad staring at you every day…"

AS AMERICAN PRIDE HITS A 25-YEAR LOW, A NEW 9/11 EDUCATION PLATFORM URGES THE NATION TO NEVER FORGET

Davidson told the Post that he’s not sure how he’ll tell his daughter about how her grandfather died. "Luckily, I have some time," he said.

"Honestly, this year is way harder than it’s been in a really long time because I have Scottie, and now I’m the age that my dad was when he died," he admitted. "So I’m just kind of like, ‘Holy s--t.’"

In 2023, Davison told the "Real Ones" podcast that his father told him he would pick him up from school on 9/11, but he was picked up by his mother, who didn’t tell him anything for three days.

He said his mom was 30 at the time. "I wouldn’t know what the f--- to do and that’s why, when I get older, I’m like, ‘Man, my mom was awesome. I was like f---, she really loves me, like d--n, like f---, that was like rough."

"She kept telling me ‘Dad’s at work, coming home,’ whatever. I had no idea."

His mom told him he was grounded and not allowed to watch TV, but he said he turned it on one night, "and I just saw my dad on TV … And they’re like ‘these are all the firemen that are like dead and all that s---."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

One thing that Davidson said frustrates him about social media is people who aren’t personally connected to the tragedy often use it as a meme.

"It’s this weird thing that happens in our country where a tragedy over time becomes a holiday," he told the Post. "And then sometimes I know the youth on the internet uses 9/11 memes as jokes. Someone will be like, ‘This song’s fire,’ and then they’ll post the towers … and we’re the ones that have to see that s--- all the time," he said.

"And it’s very nice that people that have nothing to do with it post a photo on that day, and they’ll never forget," he added. "But it’s also like, you guys have no f---ing idea, actually."

item.title: Former Mets pitcher Al Leiter tells his harrowing 9/11 story of a quiet trip turned tragedy
item.description: Al Leiter recalls his harrowing 9/11 morning, from sneaking home to walk his daughter to school to watching the twin towers burn from a cab.
item.content:encoded:
On September 11, 2001, former New York Mets pitcher Al Leiter was trying to pull off a quiet personal mission before pitching in Pittsburgh that night.

Decades later, appearing on OutKick's "The Craig Carton Show," Leiter recalled the events of that fateful morning.

His story began with a father wanting to be present for a family milestone.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Despite a scheduled game in Pittsburgh, Leiter quietly flew home to New York without informing team management.

"I wanted to be there for my daughter's first grade," Leiter said.

"She was scared. You know, 'We'll be there, honey.' And I'm like playing a long time, I'm probably 15, 16 years in the big leagues, whatever. And I knew if it wasn't Pittsburgh, US Air had like a flight like every hour, was like a shuttle. Drop her off, get on the plane."

He acknowledged breaking routine without his bosses knowing: "I never had done this, Craig. I can't believe I actually did it. I don't know if I did it like Bobby Valentine and Steve Phillips didn't know about it."

GEORGE W BUSH RECALLS MOMENT WITH DEREK JETER BEFORE NERVE-WRACKING PITCH AT YANKEE STADIUM AFTER 9/11

After walking his daughter to school, Leiter sat on the tarmac at LaGuardia Airport as initial reports trickled in.

"The pilot says, 'Oh, it looks like a news helicopter by the [World] Trade Center. We're about ready to take off,'" Leiter recalled.

"And then not five minutes later, we're going back to the airport. Get your stuff. New York airspace is closed, LaGuardia is closed, evacuate."

Even after evacuating, the true scale of the crisis hadn't set in.

"I still think we're gonna play. At that time, you know, we don't know what they're like."

Determined to reach his team, Leiter hailed a cab to head toward Philadelphia for an alternate flight.

"I called Jay Harts. I'm, 'Jay, you got to get me a flight. I'm going to Philly,'" Leiter recalled. "I have a female Pakistani cab driver. When do you ever get a female, like, and she's crying. I'm like, 'Can you take me to Philadelphia? I'll pay you.' And I'm pissed off. I'm mad. I'm sad. So going over to Triborough Bridge, the towers are burning."

As New York City shut down, Leiter rerouted north up the Major Deegan Expressway.

"They closed off New York City. I was going to go up to Tappan Zee over to go down through New Jersey to get to Philly to get on a plane to pitch that night," Leiter said. "By the time I'm on the D again, going north of Yankee Stadium, heading up to Tappan Zee, radio's on and the Pentagon just got hit."

9/11 MUSEUM UNVEILS EXHIBITION FOR GENERATION TOO YOUNG TO REMEMBER THE ATTACKS: 'CALLED EVERYBODY TO LEAD'

Leiter immediately called then-general manager Steve Phillips.

"I called Steve Phillips. I said, 'Steve, I'm sorry, but like, I'm pretty sure we're not playing baseball, right?'" Leiter added. "It's like, 'Don't worry about it.'"

Reflecting on the contrast of that morning, Leiter described the weight of the day.

"I tell you that story because you know it was so bizarrely unique for like the balls that I had actually to do that, and then that was the day of the most heinous terrorist act in the history of our country," he said.

Looking back decades later, Leiter emphasized that while public discussion surrounding the tragedy shifts, historical reality does not.

"Every year it's like my story doesn't change, right? Like history doesn't change. Although now what we're seeing, like you know I read the paper about like there were 19 Al-Qaeda guys that took down four planes. Like I'm reading stuff, there's like the story is changing. What are we doing here, right? My story's not changed."

Leiter cautioned against efforts to reshape the narrative around the tragedy.

"I think a narrative that is out there is trying to paint 9/11 in a way that I just disagree with," Leiter said. "That was a heinous terrorist act that killed 3,000 lives, right? Almost 400 firefighters running up there to help people. And so many more."

He emphasized that keeping the memory clear remains an essential duty.

"It couldn't be a simpler moniker of Never Forget, right?" Leiter stated. "And it's not just a slogan. It's true. Because it's easy, I can see how as time goes on, you start... wait a minute, that happened. Let's not forget that it happened."

item.title: Jewish campus life at a ‘crossing point’ as students weigh antisemitism risks, new report shows
item.description: Alums for Campus Fairness names the 10 most concerning and 10 most supportive campuses for Jewish students in its new 2025-26 campus climate report.
item.content:encoded:
EXCLUSIVE — The difference between a hostile and a supportive campus for Jewish students may come down to how administrators act when tensions rise, according to a new report. 

Alums for Campus Fairness (ACF) released its 2025-26 Campus Climate Brief in which it names the 10 most concerning and 10 most supportive campuses for Jewish students, along with a few "honorable mentions" in both categories.

"The schools that get it right understand their role and understand that they have an obligation to support all students, including Jewish students and Zionist students," ACF Executive Director Avi Gordon told Fox News Digital. "And I think those schools are flourishing, they’re welcoming, and it’s a place that’s desirable for certainly within the Jewish and pro-Israel community."

To evaluate each of the schools profiled in the report, ACF used five criteria: incident records, the institution's response to antisemitism, anti-Israel organizing, Jewish life on campus and an evaluation of the legal and structural environment. The report found 14 concerning campuses and 17 strong campuses across 17 states.

BIPARTISAN DUO LAUNCHES CONGRESSIONAL CAUCUS TO CONFRONT ANTISEMITISM AT COLLEGES

The 10 most concerning campuses in the report are Middlebury College, The New School, DePaul University, Smith College, Sarah Lawrence College, San Francisco State University (SFSU), University of Texas at Dallas, University of California, Berkeley, Oberlin College and George Mason University. Alums for Campus Fairness also gave "honorable mentions" to the City University of New York System, University of Washington, Occidental College and Pitzer College.

ACF profiled each of the schools, detailing antisemitic incidents, institutional responses — or lack thereof — and anti-Israel organizing, among other factors. For Middlebury College, ACF cited the university's Hillel chapter renaming itself "The Jewish Association at Middlebury," after "an attempted disaffiliation from Hillel international."

"Whatever the internal politics, the fact that national Hillel affiliation is contested at all reflects how thoroughly anti-Zionist sentiment has penetrated the campus's Jewish institutional life," ACF's report read.

According to the report, the Students for Justice in Palestine (SJP) chapter at the New School advertised a "Vigil for Martyr Yahya Sinwar," referring to the deceased leader of Hamas. ACF noted that the group continued to promote the event even after Meta removed the original post.

At UC Berkeley, "wanted" posters targeting Jewish UC regents appeared in September 2025. Then, in November 2025, "Kill all Zionists" was spray-painted in Berkeley graduate housing. The report also noted that UC Berkeley was sued by the Justice Department in February 2026 for maintaining "an antisemitic hostile work environment."

OPINION: CAMPUS ANTISEMITISM IS AN AMERICA FIRST ISSUE. ALUMNI MUST STAY IN THE FIGHT.

SFSU was included on ACF's list of most concerning campuses because of what the organization described as a broader anti-Zionist culture embedded in the university. The report cited the hosting of Mahmoud Khalil by the university's Race and Resistance Studies department and the General Union of Palestine Students.

However, SFSU disputed ACF's characterization, with Director of Communications Bobby King telling Fox News Digital via email that "SFSU has made combatting antisemitism a University priority."

King pointed to SFSU's 2022 partnership with SF Hillel, Hillel International and the Academic Engagement Network "to implement a program developed by the latter two organizations designed to combat antisemitism on college campuses."

In a recent JWeekly article, Roger Feigelson, executive director of the San Francisco Hillel that serves SFSU, called the university "a role model for how to fight antisemitism on college campuses."

Gordon said that the leadership at campuses on ACF's "most concerning" list should "address the Jewish community and need to work together with the Jewish community."

UC BERKELEY SLAMMED AFTER ANTI-ISRAEL GROUP HOSTS FAILED SUICIDE BOMBER AS GUEST EVENT SPEAKER: 'CESSPOOL'

DOJ SPRINGS ANTISEMITISM REVIEW ON BLUE STATE COLLEGE AFTER 'LEBANESE RESISTANCE' FUNDRAISER

ACF also evaluated 10 of the strongest campuses for Jewish students, which included Tulane University, University of Florida, Vanderbilt University, University of Miami, Brandeis University, Indiana University, Arizona State University, Binghamton University, Dartmouth College and University of Southern California. It also gave "honorable mentions" to Washington University in St. Louis, Emory University, University of Georgia, University of Central Florida, Boston University, University of Arizona and Yeshiva University.

In a statement provided to Fox News Digital, the University of Southern California (USC) said that the designation reflected "the concrete steps USC has taken to support our Jewish community."

"At USC, we want every student — of every background, faith, and perspective — to know they are welcome and valued. We are proud that Alums for Campus Fairness has ranked USC among the top ten campuses for Jewish students, and the only California university on the list," the statement read.

Gordon, a graduate of Binghamton University, said that something his alma mater gets right is its relationship with Jewish institutions. The ACF report notes that Binghamton has weekly meetings involving administrators and representatives from Hillel and Chabad.

ACF calls Binghamton "the campus where BDS went backwards," noting that while a boycott, divestment and sanctions resolution passed in April 2024, it was rescinded months later in October 2024. Additionally, in January 2025, the Student Assembly Congress posted a statement condemning divestment from Israel.

The ACF executive director also pointed to Vanderbilt University as a "great example" of a school that is getting it right. In ACF's report, it is noted that Vanderbilt did not have any recorded antisemitic incidents in the 2025-26 academic year. Additionally, it praised the university for its swift action in February 2026 after a mathematics lecturer was reported for embedding anti-Israel content in course materials.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

Gordon told Fox News Digital that ACF is not looking for censorship, noting that the free exchange of ideas is still a vital part of the college experience. However, he said the issue arises when Jewish students experience intimidation, vandalism and bigotry.

When asked about what the report means as a whole, Gordon said it shows that Jewish life on American campuses is at a crucial moment.

"I think Jewish life on campus is at a kind of crossing point. I think that Jewish students are becoming way more acutely aware of what the risks are when deciding to apply to a university and what risks they're willing to take or not," Gordon told Fox News Digital.

"I think these schools must understand kind of the reality of the students on the ground, the reality of potential students as well, and the role that alumni have to play in kind of sharing those views with the administration as well," he added. "You know, alumni have a seat at the table, and we want to be able to help them understand what's going on campus in a more fine, granular way."

Fox News Digital reached out to all institutions mentioned in Alums for Campus Fairness' report for comment but did not immediately receive responses. Occidental College and University of Central Florida declined to comment.

item.title: I witnessed the horror of 9/11 firsthand. Here's what I learned about God, courage and life
item.description: A 9/11 survivor who witnessed the World Trade Center attack from an adjacent building shares how that day led her to become an FBI special agent.
item.content:encoded:
Tuesday, 8:46 a.m., September 11, 2001, changed my life — and the lives of millions of others — forever. Nineteen hijackers from the terrorist organization al Qaeda carried out the devil’s work, resulting in the murder of 2,977 innocent souls who were never able to fulfill the measure of their creation. I witnessed the horror unfold up close while working at Merrill Lynch on the top floor of the World Financial Center, adjacent to the World Trade Center (WTC) in New York City.

When I heard the loudest explosion, I rushed to the window and saw a gaping hole, chunks of the silver metallic building falling like confetti, massive flames and black smoke billowing from the North Tower (1 WTC). I could not process what I was seeing. I had walked through 1 WTC only an hour earlier. My first thought was: "People are dying up there." My heart was crushed as the terror continued.

After I watched the second plane slam into the South Tower (2 WTC), I knew we were under attack. I frantically escaped my building. Amid the pandemonium, a sobering question came to mind. For a moment, time stood still, and I asked myself: If I were to die today, am I prepared to meet my Maker? Am I ready to die?

FRANK SILLER: 'I LOVE YOU, BROTHER' -- THE 9/11 LOSS THAT INSPIRED A MISSION OF SERVICE

Through the fear and terror, I experienced a glimmer of peace as I dug deep to make sense of the mayhem. One thing I knew for certain: I was a child of God, and He loved me. I felt that calm reassurance even in the darkness. There was hope. I instantly knew I was at the WTC for a reason. Right then, I vowed that I would stand as a witness for God, serve others and serve our great nation.

I stayed true to that vow and left the lucrative financial industry in 2009 to serve as an FBI special agent.

9/11 MUSEUM UNVEILS EXHIBITION FOR GENERATION TOO YOUNG TO REMEMBER THE ATTACKS: 'CALLED EVERYBODY TO LEAD'

I witnessed the best and worst of humanity on 9/11. Selflessness, sacrifice, and courage were on full display among the FDNY, NYPD, the Port Authority Police Department, first responders and everyday civilians who perished protecting strangers. These patriots ran toward danger while everyone else ran away. Passengers on United Flight 93 bravely prevented the plane from reaching its intended target.

We also pay tribute to the thousands of rescue and recovery workers who have since died from health issues resulting from exposure to Ground Zero toxins. No words adequately express the praise these heroes deserve. May all those murdered on 9/11 rest in peace, and may God comfort their loved ones who continue to live with unimaginable loss. The hijackers destroyed towers and killed thousands, but the spirits of those we lost are eternal and will live on forever.

9/11 HERO WELLES CROWTHER'S FIREHOUSE PRESIDENT REVEALS WHAT SHAPED THE 'MAN IN THE RED BANDANA'

The leadership of New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani was remarkable. It was inspiring to see New York City, the U.S., and the entire world unite in compassion and empathy. There was never a time when we were prouder to be Americans living in the greatest country in the world.

We must call 9/11 exactly what it was: an attack on America by terrorists who despised our freedom and way of life. We must never forget this catastrophe so that history does not repeat itself. New Yorkers are resilient. The terrorists did not win. Yet in 2026, it is unconscionable that fellow Americans proclaim that the U.S. and the blameless victims deserved 9/11. Abhorrent. The moral decline and erosion of the sanctity of human life are alarming.

LIZ PEEK: WE CANNOT LET THE LEFT REWRITE WHAT HAPPENED ON 9/11

I was barely 23 years old then, and 25 years later, 9/11 remains the single most impactful day of my life. The trauma changes you. That living nightmare will remain seared in my mind forever: the gruesome images, acrid smell, carnage, crashing sounds, blaring sirens, and the sight of victims jumping to their deaths out of sheer desperation because it was their only option.

Witnessing countless people die horrific deaths taught me invaluable lessons about living. Tell people you love them often; you never know when it could be your last goodbye. Life is a fragile gift. One second, you’re here, and the next, you may be gone.

I LOST MY WIFE ON 9/11. PLEASE LET THIS 25TH ANNIVERSARY BELONG TO THE FAMILIES

Don’t sweat the small stuff. Careers, net worth, notoriety, titles, wealth, possessions and power don’t go with you when you leave this earth. Make a positive difference with the talents, gifts and abundance you’ve been blessed with. Where much is given, much is required. Never be so consumed with inconsequential busyness that you don’t have time to show up for others. True joy and purpose come from easing another’s burden.

Live fearlessly. Don’t become paralyzed by turmoil. Rather than becoming bitter or angry, channel the energy from trauma toward good. Never be a victim. Even amid chaos, it’s possible to feel inner peace.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Forgive. Show compassion. Be grateful. Exercise faith. Do unto others as you’d have them do unto you. Maintain your integrity regardless of the pressures around you.

Life is short. Make it count. Have no regrets or what-ifs. Take risks. Live fully.

Pray. God knows and loves you. He is there for you.

The most powerful lesson I learned on 9/11 is that a literal battle between good and evil is underway. Standing on the sidelines is no longer an option. Pick your side. Spread light. Live a life of honor. Even amid what can seem like complete moral decay, I can unequivocally declare that, in the end, light will conquer darkness.

Good. Will. Win.

In God, we trust.

9/11 — Never Forget.

item.title: Former Michigan hockey players allege coaches ignored years of abusive hazing rituals
item.description: Sixteen former University of Michigan hockey players allege freshmen endured forced genital shaving, excessive drinking and blowtorch hazing rituals.
item.content:encoded:
Sixteen former University of Michigan men’s hockey players filed a federal sex discrimination lawsuit in Detroit, alleging they were subjected to sexual abuse and hazing rituals as members of the program between 1984 and 2001.

The complaint alleges freshmen endured forced genital shaving, excessive drinking and being made to eat live fish as part of team initiation. One player also alleged that upperclassmen taunted him with a blowtorch while he lay on a table.

The former players’ attorney, Michael Pitt, described the alleged team culture.

"The abuse was ritualized, meticulously planned, and sadistic," Pitt said. "Enduring sexual abuse was required to be a member of the Michigan Men’s Ice Hockey team."

The lawsuit accused Red Berenson, Michigan’s head coach from 1984 to 2017, of knowing about the alleged abuse and failing to intervene.

One former player, identified as John Doe 3, allegedly told Berenson he wanted no part in the hazing. The complaint claims Berenson pressured him to participate by invoking the ideals of being a "Michigan Man" and a "good teammate."

Berenson, 86, has disputed allegations of coaching involvement. He previously acknowledged that senior players oversaw some initiation practices, while maintaining that no one had complained to him.

"Were there some mishaps? Were there some bad experiences? Possibly, but it wasn’t a matter of direction or encouragement from the coaching staff or from the administration," Berenson said.

He also disputed the lawsuit’s characterization of the alleged conduct.

"When they say sexual, I’m guessing they’re stretching this," Berenson said.

Berenson announced the end of "freshman hazing" in 2012. At the time, he primarily referred to first-year players being forced to carry equipment and eat team meals last. He also acknowledged that some "captains got too carried away."

The former players’ lawsuit argues that Berenson’s comments should have prompted Michigan to investigate the team’s hazing practices.

Michigan spokesperson Paul Corliss called the allegations "disturbing" but denied that the university was responsible for the alleged misconduct.

"To the extent any former student-athlete engaged in hazing or other misconduct, they were violating university policy," Corliss said.

"The university first adopted an official anti-hazing policy in 1982. It was one of the first universities in the country to do so, and it has earned its standing as a leader in this area," he added.

The allegations surfaced after former players began discussing their experiences in 2024. Michigan could argue that the former players waited too long to file the lawsuit because the alleged abuse occurred decades ago.

The university made a similar argument in litigation involving former athletes who accused campus sports doctor Robert Anderson of sexual misconduct. Michigan ultimately agreed to pay $490 million to settle claims involving more than 1,000 former athletes. The allegations in the hockey lawsuit have not been proven in court.

item.title: Putin, Xi and Iran's Pezeshkian descend on India for high-stakes BRICS summit amid escalating global tensions
item.description: Presidents of Iran, Russia and China converge on New Delhi for the BRICS summit as India navigates competing interests amid Middle East and Ukraine wars.
item.content:encoded:
All eyes will be on New Delhi this weekend, as the presidents of Iran, Russia and China gather in India for the 18th BRICS summit. The meeting comes at a critical time as conflicts roil the Middle East and Europe, putting the bloc to one of its biggest tests since its founding 20 years ago.

The Sept. 12-13 summit comes more than six months after the Middle East war broke out between the U.S. and Iran, and at a time when regional tensions are again spiking. It follows the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) summit earlier this month, where several of the same leaders met.

The BRICS alliance was established in 2006 by founding members Brazil, Russia, India and China, and has since expanded to include nations such as Iran, Egypt, Ethiopia, Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates.

INDIA'S MODI-IRAN MEETING COMES AMID US WARNINGS OF SANCTIONS ON TEHRAN'S TRADING PARTNERS

At the forefront are Iran-India relations, with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and Prime Minister Narendra Modi likely to highlight trade, connectivity, energy cooperation and regional developments. The two leaders are meeting less than two weeks after reaffirming their "longstanding" strategic partnership.

In the face of an economic onslaught from Washington, Tehran has been working to deepen ties with Moscow and Beijing. In its latest attempt at securing a critical economic lifeline, Iran is seeking membership in the BRICS New Development Bank. The effort comes as many of Iran's largest remaining economic partners, including China, India, Russia and the UAE, will all be represented in New Delhi, giving Tehran a rare opportunity to engage several key trading partners collectively, just as the U.S. ramps up sanctions pressure.

CHINA, RUSSIA, IRAN AND NORTH KOREA FORM 'AXIS OF AGGRESSORS' THAT COULD OVERWHELM US, BOOK WARNS

Also in focus is China. President Xi Jinping will be visiting India for the first time in seven years. The high-stakes trip marks the biggest step yet in a cautious thaw between India and China after a deadly military clash in 2020 along their disputed Himalayan border. A bilateral meeting between Modi and Xi is expected to focus on maintaining that normalization while expanding economic engagement, making it one of the summit's most closely watched sidelines meetings.

Then there is Russia. President Vladimir Putin met Modi on Friday in a pre-summit bilateral meeting. It marks Putin's first trip to India since the Ukraine war began four years ago.

Energy and defense are expected to dominate the agenda after the Russian president criticized American tariffs as "illegal" and "unacceptable."

Just earlier this week, the Kremlin touted expanding energy ties, saying India's imports of Russian energy have reached a "new record" every month. Moscow has also said Russia understands India's position on the war in Ukraine and that it "to a great extent corresponds" with Russia's own position, while calling on India to facilitate a peaceful resolution.

IRAN LOSES KEY ECONOMIC LIFELINE IN MIDDLE EAST THAT TRUMP'S SANCTIONS COULDN'T REACH AS DEADLOCK PERSISTS

The meeting also comes days after Putin publicly welcomed the UAE’s role in facilitating discussions over the Ukraine war, highlighting Abu Dhabi's increasingly influential diplomatic role as another major BRICS participant.

Saudi Arabia will also be watched after Iran-backed Houthi militia renewed attacks on its cities earlier this week.

Both the UAE and Saudi Arabia have become increasingly central to India's Gulf strategy. The summit also comes as New Delhi attempts to navigate widening divisions between Tehran and Abu Dhabi after the UAE cut off commercial and financial dealings with Iran. The suspension has already squeezed Indian exporters, as Dubai has long served as a key commercial hub for India's trade with Iran, giving India a direct economic incentive.

The BRICS summit will be a major test of India's diplomatic mettle in more ways than one, as the nation finds itself balancing competing interests from Washington, Tehran, Moscow, Beijing and the Gulf while trying to forge unity among BRICS members.

"New Delhi’s leadership of BRICS is ultimately an exercise in managing contradiction. The biggest challenge is to ensure BRICS remains a platform for advancing Global South priorities rather than becoming an arena for great-power rivalry, Harsh V. Pant, vice president at Observer Research Foundation, told Fox News Digital. "New Delhi is trying to keep the focus on practical cooperation — from energy security to connectivity and development — rather than ideological confrontation."

FROM BEAR HUGS TO HANDSHAKES: HOW INDIA LOST ITS EDGE WITH TRUMP WHILE PAKISTAN QUIETLY GAINED GROUND

Building a unified position among BRICS members will be a complex task for India, especially given the sharp geopolitical divergences among member states, such as the U.S-China rivalry, the Russia-Ukraine war and tensions involving Iran, Israel and the UAE. Modi will have to balance championing his own priorities with the summit's, as well as toeing the line to avoid an anti-U.S. tilt.

"The balancing act reflects India's broader foreign policy, which seeks to maintain strong ties with Washington while continuing to engage Moscow, Beijing and Tehran," Pant said.

Throughout the conflict, India has sought to position itself as a voice for dialogue while avoiding taking sides, emphasizing themes of resilience, sustainability, cooperation and innovation.

But experts warn that failure to reach consensus would expose the limits of the expanded BRICS grouping, whose broader membership has also imported longstanding regional rivalries.

Though major Western powers are absent, analysts say the alliance is not to be dismissed. Every ceasefire in this conflict has involved mediation by BRICS members or partners, and leaders gathering in New Delhi are expected to explore whether the forum can once again provide diplomatic momentum after recent attempts to revive negotiations between Washington and Tehran stalled.

"Hosting the BRICS summit in New Delhi offers India an important opportunity to demonstrate the logic of its multi-alignment at a time when global politics is becoming increasingly polarized, "Pant said. "By bringing together countries such as China, Russia, Iran and the Gulf states while simultaneously deepening its partnerships with the United States and the Quad, India is signaling that it does not accept the binary choices imposed by great-power rivalry."

The stakes extend beyond diplomacy as disruptions from the war have disproportionately affected developing nations. India, the world's third-largest oil importer and consumer, has already suffered energy and inflation hits. 

"The real measure of India’s success will therefore be its ability to keep BRICS sufficiently inclusive and functional to address Global South priorities while preventing geopolitical divisions from paralyzing the grouping," Pant said.

item.title: Powerhouse college football team throttles FCS team so violently, both coaches agreed to shorten the game
item.description: Darian Mensah threw three touchdowns with just one incompletion as the Miami Hurricanes demolished Florida A&M 77-7 in a historic rout game.
item.content:encoded:
The No. 7 Miami Hurricanes throttled FCS Florida A&M so badly in Thursday night's home-opener, both teams agreed to wave the white flag at the start of the fourth quarter.

This is probably why FBS and FCS teams should never be on the same field together again — especially not in today's world of transfer portal madness and NIL.

The Hurricanes won 77-7. It was never close. It was never even kind of close. This game got out of hand so quickly, the scoreboard had a hard time keeping up.

Miami went up 14-0 before the game was five minutes old. The Hurricanes scored a touchdown on all seven first half possessions. They scored four more touchdown in the third quarter.

FAMU had two first downs the entire first half. The Rattlers quarterback was hit so hard on the game's third play, it went viral on social media.

Miami's Heismen-hopeful QB, Darian Mensah, threw for three touchdowns and one incompletion. One.

The Hurricanes' backup QB went 8 for 8 with three more touchdowns.

The THIRD stringer threw one incompletion.

As a team, Miami ran for more than 400 yards.

So, yes, the 'Canes won this game, 77-7. They could've scored 100 points if they wanted. Maybe 200.

Both coaches agree to call the dogs off before the fourth quarter:

Thoughts? First impressions?

Here's mine: If both teams need to agree, in the third quarter, to shorten the fourth quarter, because the game is so absurdly out of hand ... those teams shouldn't have been on the same field in the first place.

It's pretty simple.

I understand why this game was necessary. For FAMU, it was about a check. A literal paycheck. That's what they went to Miami Gardens for Thursday night.

I don't know how much Miami paid them, but was it worth the national embarrassment? I guess so, given these low-level FCS teams continue to play these national championship contenders every single year. It helps the athletic department.

Frankly, it probably funds them for the rest of the school year. Again, I get it.

But at some point, it's just bad for the game. It's a bad look. The talent discrepancy is shocking, especially in today's world.

Some years, FAMU would be able to keep this thing respectable because the 'Canes would've been in a terrible recruiting cycle. I've seen it happen.

Years ago, in a previous life, I covered Bethune-Cookman's trip to Miami. The Wildcats — another HBCU team, just like FAMU — lost, 42-13. It was never close, but it was never out of hand.

But that will never, ever be the case anymore because college athletics is all about NIL and the transfer portal. That's it. It's almost impossible for one of these powerhouses to have a down year.

So this game — along with tomorrow's Campbell Fighting Camels-Florida Gators game in Gainesville — will forever look like this:

My God. What a bloodbath. Again, Miami could've hung 100 on them. The 'Canes tried! Mario Cristobal went for it on 4th and 7 from the FAMU 8 with two minutes to go!

item.title: Lost city where Jesus performed miracles has finally been identified, expert says
item.description: Bethsaida, the home of Apostle Peter and the setting of Jesus Christ's miracles, may finally be identified after a decade of archaeology work at El-Araj.
item.content:encoded:
Archaeologists believe they've identified a lost city tied to Jesus Christ's ministry after a decade of excavations, with the project's academic director saying he's "100%" certain about the discovery.

The El-Araj Excavation Project, led by Mordechai Aviam, has been digging at the archaeological site along the Sea of Galilee since 2016.

Bethsaida, close to Jesus' ministry in Capernaum, was once the home of the apostles Peter, Andrew and Philip.

AUTHOR DINESH D'SOUZA CHALLENGES BIBLE SKEPTICS WITH 'STARTLING' ARCHAEOLOGICAL DISCOVERIES

The city was the setting of several of Jesus' miracles, including the healing of a blind man.

Jesus' feeding of the 5,000 took place on Bethsaida's outskirts, according to the Gospels.

Over the past decade, researchers have uncovered extensive evidence of an ancient Jewish fishing settlement and Roman-era city at the El-Araj site.

This year's excavation opened new areas of the site, revealing additional Roman period remains and pottery, Steven Notley, a biblical scholar and academic director of the El-Araj Excavation Project, told Fox News Digital.

ANCIENT BOOK OF REVELATION CITY GIVES UP STUNNING SECRET BURIED FOR 1,500 YEARS

Researchers have also recovered over 200 coins, which are being studied to help date the settlement.

Notley, dean of religious studies at Pillar College in New Jersey, said an unexpected wildfire last year helped researchers gain a better understanding of the size of the ancient settlement.

"We actually had a wildfire, which at first we thought was tragic," Notley said. "But it actually cleared the underbrush and allowed us to do an extended survey to determine the size of the settlement. It's at least 15 acres."

The team has also uncovered Jewish stone vessels, a Roman bathhouse and a Byzantine basilica containing an inscription linked to the Apostle Peter.

LOST CITY TIED TO BIBLICAL EXODUS MAY HAVE FINALLY BEEN DISCOVERED IN EGYPT

Notley indicated that researchers looking for Bethsaida would expect to find evidence of two things: a Jewish fishing village and its later transformation into a small Roman city.

Excavations at El-Araj have revealed evidence of both, he said, including thousands of lead fishing weights, stone vessels associated with Jewish settlement and the remains of a Roman bathhouse.

"The two things that we should be finding if we're excavating that sort of coincide with that identification are a Jewish fishing village which, again, we've found ample evidence of that and evidence of a polis of urbanization," Notley said.

After a decade of excavations, Notley is now "100%" confident that El-Araj is Bethsaida, he told Fox News Digital.

ARCHAEOLOGISTS UNEARTH SECRET CHURCH TIED TO COUNCIL OF NICAEA, CHRISTIANITY'S DEFINING MOMENT

Rather than a single discovery proving the site's identity, Notley said the case for Bethsaida has been built over years of excavation.

"It's [the] accumulation of evidence that you continually find," he said.

"Since 2016, we have not uncovered a single thing that would challenge or question the identification of the site as Bethsaida," Notley added. "Instead, everything we find each season, the evidence gets stronger and stronger and strong."

In the Byzantine basilica, excavators found an inscription referencing "the Chief of the Apostles and the Keeper of the Keys of Heaven," or the Apostle Peter.

Researchers also found Roman-period homes beneath the church, which Notley said was traditionally believed to have been built over the home of Peter and Andrew.

"Can you be absolutely certain this is Peter's home? No, I can't say that," Notley said.

"You're not going to find a plaque that says, ‘Peter slept here, Peter lived here.’ But in archaeological terms, it's about as good as you can get."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Bethsaida's ties to Jesus are what make the find particularly significant.

"Of course, for Christians, there are a number of stories from the Gospels about Jesus being present in Bethsaida," Notley said.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"At least one quarter of Jesus' disciples come from Bethsaida. So it's an important site in his life, in his ministry," he added.

And after a decade of digging, Notley said there is still more to uncover.

"I'm looking forward to what lies ahead," he added.

item.title: Massachusetts' highest court publicly reprimands judge accused of enabling immigrant to escape ICE
item.description: Judge Shelley Joseph was publicly rebuked after an illegal immigrant evaded Immigration and Customs Enforcement in her Massachusetts courtroom.
item.content:encoded:
The highest court in Massachusetts has publicly rebuked a district court judge over her role in a case involving an illegal immigrant who evaded arrest by Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

For Judge Shelley Joseph, the decision brings to a close a legal saga that began on April 2, 2018, when Jose Medina-Perez left the Newton District Court through a rear courthouse exit all while an ICE officer was waiting in the lobby to take him into custody.

The Supreme Judicial Court's ruling centered on a sidebar with Medina-Perez's attorney and the prosecutor during which Joseph instructed her clerk to shut off the courtroom's recording system.

"The respondent's statements during that conversation, including her proposal to detain Medina-Perez overnight in State custody, and her conduct in instructing the clerk to turn off the courtroom audio recording system, created an appearance of impropriety in violation of her duties," according to the Thursday ruling from the Supreme Judicial Court.

FORMER WISCONSIN JUDGE HANNAH DUGAN AVOIDS JAIL TIME FOR OBSTRUCTING ARREST OF ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT

The Supreme Judicial Court's reprimand came after a hearing officer for the Commission on Judicial Conduct recommended such an action.

However, the high court ruled that Joseph was unaware Medina-Perez's attorney, David Jellinek, had devised a plan to help his client evade ICE by escorting him to the courthouse lockup, where the court officer would release him through a rear sally port exit. The court also found that Joseph neither explicitly nor implicitly approved of that plan.

Medina-Perez, of the Dominican Republic, had been in Joseph's courtroom to be arraigned on a fugitive-from-justice charge that originated in Pennsylvania.

Joseph found there wasn't enough evidence to tie Medina-Perez to the Pennsylvania warrant, and prosecutor Shannon Jurgens recommended he be released without bail on two drug charges he was facing.

FEDERAL JUDGE IN NEW YORK TIES TRUMP ADMIN HANDS ON ARRESTS AT IMMIGRATION COURTS

Joseph then released Medina-Perez on his own personal recognizance and set a pre-trial conference date for the drug possession case.

In April 2019, roughly a year later, Joseph and the court officer who let Medina-Perez out through the back door were indicted on charges of obstruction of justice.

That case was dropped in 2022 after Joseph agreed to refer herself to the Commission on Judicial Conduct, the agency that investigates allegations of misconduct by Massachusetts judges.

The commission concluded that Joseph "engaged in willful judicial misconduct that brought the judicial office into disrepute, as well as conduct prejudicial to the administration of justice and unbecoming a judicial officer."

After her federal indictment, Joseph was suspended from the bench and unable to work for three years.

Joseph's attorney, Elizabeth Mulvey, said last year during a commission hearing that the case had been distorted in the media, with many coming to believe that her client "let an illegal immigrant out of the door," according to The Associated Press.

In a statement to the AP on Thursday, Mulvey said it has been an "incredibly long and difficult eight years for Judge Joseph."

"We are grateful to the hearing officer who undertook this monumental task and pleased that his efforts have shown that this was a baseless federal prosecution from the beginning and solely the work of the defense lawyer involved," Mulvey said in a statement. "Judge Joseph is thankful for everyone who stood by her and looks forward to rejoining her colleagues."

Joseph, who remains a judge, was assigned in December to administrative duties in the Boston Municipal Court.

item.title: DR MARC SIEGEL: Twenty-five years after 9/11, the deadly health crisis is still claiming lives
item.description: A physician who helped empty Bellevue Hospital on 9/11 details how World Trade Center cancer cases have jumped 75% between 2023 and 2025 alone.
item.content:encoded:
When the alerts came on September 11, 2001, I first made sure my kids were safe and then headed to home base, which for me was that concrete lifesaver – Bellevue Hospital. I helped empty the hospital where I had trained, triaging patients to other facilities in preparation for World Trade Center survivors. Then we waited for hours for survivors who never came.

A few days later I visited the disaster site, and when I arrived, I was handed an N95 mask. I made my way through the rubble, very aware that I was in the presence of potentially toxic chemicals and fumes. It was a bright, sunny day, but there was still a film in the air.

With all due respect to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, who is claiming the public was lied to and has released 170,000 documents related to the attacks to supposedly verify a coverup, I have a simple response.

MAMDANI DROPS MASSIVE 9/11 RECORDS TROVE AS OLD CLAIMS ABOUT GROUND ZERO COME UNDER FIRE

We knew.

We knew there were potentially serious health risks.

We knew the molten debris and toxins were a problem. We knew that there would be health risks and consequences from the terror attacks for generations to come, not only for first responders—heroes who put their lives on the line to try to save the few people they could—but also for survivors and the people who lived in the surrounding New York City neighborhoods.

REPORTER’S NOTEBOOK: 9/11 IS JUST A HISTORY CHAPTER FOR A NEW GENERATION OF AMERICANS

Over the years, I have treated many patients with health consequences from direct exposure, from gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) to asthma, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and cancer. Many have come to me who simply lived in the neighborhood and were rightfully worried that their symptoms could be connected to that exposure.

I have shared patients with the well-designed and executed World Trade Center Health Program, which has helped monitor my patients with CT scans of the chest and other screening tools.

Over the years, it has become clearer that increased cancer rates have been tied directly to the toxins released into the air that fateful day. The Northwell WTC Health Program has revealed that 57,000 cancer cases have been linked to 9/11 toxic debris. Cases have jumped 75% from 2023 to 2025 alone. There has been a twofold increase in lung cancer in just five years. Skin, prostate, breast, and thyroid cancers, as well as lymphomas, are the most common.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION

Monitoring continues, and the trends continue to increase. More than 9,000 people have died from health-related effects of 9/11, far more than died in the attacks themselves.

As I have written previously, the American psyche was punctured on 9/11 in a way that changed us forever. Here in New York, in some ways we are stronger, but we are also more fearful. The physical and emotional impact of that day lingers today.

We knew about these risks, though the extent of the impact was far greater than anyone realized at the time, whether patient, doctor, or public health official.

How could we know? We could only predict, screen, and treat.

item.title: NFL allows stolen land acknowledgement disguised as a welcoming ceremony before Australia game
item.description: Aunty Joy Murphy Wandin's leaf ritual and 60,000-year indigenous stolen land acknowledgement preceded the NFL's first Melbourne game at the MCG.
item.content:encoded:
The most off-putting thing about the NFL asking two teams to fly 16 hours to the other side of the world and play a key division rivalry game in Australia the first week of the season was the league agreeing to give the performative antics of some lady named Aunty Joy Murphy Wandin a stage during its pregame ceremony.

Aunty Joy, as she is affectionately called by her followers, which include people in the Australian government, is an Indigenous Australian and Senior Wurundjeri elder of the Kulin Alliance, Victoria.

And what that title means is that she is often tasked with giving the traditional Welcome to Country greeting at many Melbourne, Australia events.

SOLD OUT MELBOURNE CROWD STANDS FOR 25TH ANNIVERSARY COMMEMORATION OF 9/11 AT NFL'S FIRST AUSTRALIA GAME

Except a welcome to country greeting from Aunty Joy isn't actually a welcome. It's a stolen land acknowledgement lecture during which she makes it clear that the land the visitors are on doesn't belong to White Australians.

It belongs to whatever Aboriginal or Torres Strait Islander that first inhabited the land thousands of years ago. It was 60,000 years ago, if you believe Aunty Joy's speech at the Melbourne Cricket Ground before Thursday's game.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

And the obvious question one might ask is why the NFL would accept this narrative being part of what was otherwise a solemn and respectful 9/11 pregame memorial featuring both Americans and Australians?

Why make the Netflix audience at home, not to mention the teams standing on the sidelines waiting for kickoff, listen to this stolen land gibberish?

And, let there be no doubt, it was gibberish meant to finger-wag and lecture Whitey.

During her history lesson disguised as a welcome, Aunty Joy thanked the NFL and both participating teams. She thanked the San Francisco 49ers and the Los Angeles Chargers, um, Rams.

That's right, the stolen land acknowledgement lady initially thanked the wrong Los Angeles team that wasn't present and has actually moved in to the Rams' home market after departing San Diego.

"Kulin Nation and neighboring islands … We pay our respects to your culture and heritage and those watching at home," Wandin said. "And we also thank the National Football League for bringing the San Francisco 49ers and the Los Angeles Char-Rams to 'Naarm to celebrate their first-ever flag session for this season."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Naarm, by the way, is the Indigenous name for Melbourne. Except Aunty Joy doesn't use that name – kind of like the Soviets didn't use St. Petersburg so they called it Leningrad.

"We hope that everyone enjoys themselves," she continued. "We also hope that you have enjoyed our celebration of honoring 60,000 years of our culture, and we thank all of our community who have been involved.

"We are known as the Manangan people, and I'll take this leaf on behalf of our community, the Wurundjeri Woiwurrung, and our neighboring islands."

That's when Aunty Joy plucked a leaf from a dying plant she was holding and symbolically offered it up like some pagan ritual.

"Accepting this gift means that you are welcome to everything from the tops of the trees to the roots of the earth," she said. "Wominjeka, Wurundjeri Baluk, and on my father's land, we sincerely hope you have a wonderful time here at the MCG. Wominjeka. Welcome."

Stolen land acknowledgements are apparently a thing in Australia because the people who own the land now apparently feel guilty that the people who owned it thousands of years ago no longer do.

Well, they don't feel that guilty because nobody is offering to give their land back. But they want you to feel guilty, anyway. So, yes, all performative.

What makes this strange is the NFL's collaboration. Look, it's one thing to visit historical locales and participate in cultural events in the weeks or days leading up to an international game.

But once the gameday lights go hot, nobody tunes in to hear white people get portrayed as usurpers.

And if the NFL wants to hear that, perhaps it should hold such presentations at its league office in Manhattan. You know, the New York borough settlers purchased from natives and nobody is giving back.
